t: Leonardo was working on a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo by October 1503, but he never gave the painting to her family, and he may have continued to work on it as late as 1517.
The portrait was one of the first Italian portraits to set the sitter before an imaginary landscape, and Raphael borrowed from its composition within a few years.
It passed to Francis I of France, hung in the Louvre from 1797 and became widely known partly through its theft in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, who believed it should belong to Italy.
dyk: A marginal note of October 1503 in a 1477 printing of Cicero, found in 2005 by a scholar at Heidelberg University, likens Leonardo to the Greek painter Apelles and says he was then working on a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo.
ev: A note by Agostino Vespucci records that Leonardo was working on a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo
King Francis I of France acquired the painting after Leonardo's death
The painting went on permanent display at the Louvre
Jean-Marie Hooghstoel carried out the first and most extensive recorded cleaning and revarnishing
Vincenzo Peruggia, a Louvre employee, stole the painting
The painting, recovered after Peruggia tried to sell it in Florence, returned to the Louvre
A rock thrown by Ugo Ungaza Villegas shattered the glass case and dislodged a speck of pigment near the left elbow
After conservation and study, the painting was moved to a purpose-built enclosure in the Salle des États

f.made: Leonardo da Vinci, probably for the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo and his wife Lisa, though some scholars name a different commission; Leonardo never gave it to the Giocondo family
f.form: A half-length portrait in oil on a white poplar panel, showing a seated woman in three-quarter profile before a landscape, painted without outlines in the soft blending called sfumato
f.where: The Louvre, Paris, where it has normally been on display since 1797, in a climate-controlled enclosure behind bulletproof glass in the Salle des États
f.known: the sitter's ambiguous expression; sfumato modelling; an imaginary landscape behind the figure; Leonardo's long work on it; the theft of 1911; its influence on later portraits and on avant-garde parody
